title: Can Hyperthermia Unveil Brugada Pattern?
case_prompt:
A 61-year-old man with a history of congestive heart failure, dementia, intellectual disability, and hypertension was brought to the emergency department with altered mental status and shortness of breath. His home medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, chlorthalidone, and furosemide. On arrival, his temperature was 40.4 °C, heart rate 133 bpm, respiratory rate 24 breaths/min, blood pressure 116/61 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation 94% on 4 L/min. He appeared toxic and lethargic and was nonverbal. Examination revealed a regular tachycardia and left lower extremity circumferential erythema and warmth.

Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 11.6×10^9/L, hemoglobin 11.5 g/dL, platelets 104×10^9/L, normal electrolytes, creatinine 1.9 mg/dL (baseline 1.2 mg/dL), normal TSH and free T4, and an initial high-sensitivity troponin of 126 ng/L that trended downward on repeat. A respiratory pathogen panel was positive for influenza B, lactic acid was 1.8 mmol/L, and one blood culture grew coagulase-negative staphylococci (considered contaminant).

An initial electrocardiogram during the febrile episode showed coved ST-segment elevations followed by inverted T waves in leads V1–V2, consistent with a type 1 Brugada pattern. After administration of antipyretics, a repeat ECG demonstrated resolution of the ST-segment elevations in leads V1–V2.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. ST-elevation myocardial infarction — “EKG changes concerning for STEMI … STEMI team was not activated as the EKG changes were thought to be consistent with the Brugada type 1 EKG pattern in the setting of hyperthermia and sepsis.”  
2. Brugada syndrome — “definitive diagnosis of BrS cannot be made yet” because “our patient did not have any prior history of ventricular arrhythmias, unexplained syncope, or FH of SCD.”  
3. Brugada electrocardiographic pattern secondary to fever — “EKG on presentation … showed evidence of a Brugada pattern … and repeated EKG … showed resolution of ST changes” indicating a fever-induced ECG pattern rather than a fixed disorder.
